nameStory: The 'eggleaf' in this spurge's name comes from its oval-shaped leaves that resemble tiny eggs attached to the stem. The word 'spurge' itself comes from the old French 'espurgier,' meaning 'to purge,' referring to the traditional medicinal use of these plants as strong laxatives. With only one recorded observation in all of New England, this European immigrant is quite the botanical rarity here!
description: Eggleaf spurge is a hairy perennial herb that grows up to about 20 inches tall, making it a medium-sized member of the spurge family. This European native has distinctive oval leaves with tiny teeth along their edges and produces clusters of small, inconspicuous flowers. The entire plant has a somewhat fuzzy, soft appearance due to its hairy coating. Like all spurges, it contains a milky white sap that can irritate skin.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval-shaped leaves 1.5-2.5 inches long with finely toothed edges that feel slightly rough to the touch. They're arranged alternately along the stem and have a green to yellow-green color.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows as a hairy perennial herb reaching just over 1.5 feet tall. The entire plant feels soft and fuzzy when you brush against it due to fine hairs covering stems and leaves.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny, inconspicuous flowers clustered together in small inflorescences. The flowers lack showy petals and instead have small glands that may appear yellowish-green.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round capsules about 0.2 inches across that split open to release smooth, brown seeds. The capsules feel firm and slightly bumpy when mature.

idTips.label: Sap
idTips.description: Breaks stems or leaves to reveal milky white latex sap that's characteristic of all spurges. This sap can cause skin irritation, so avoid direct contact.

habitat: As an extremely rare species in New England with only one recorded observation, eggleaf spurge's specific habitat preferences here are unclear. In its native Europe, it typically grows in disturbed soils, waste areas, and along roadsides. If encountered in New England, it would likely be in similar weedy habitats or possibly escaped from cultivation.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges with the characteristic oval, toothed leaves becoming visible. The fuzzy texture of young stems and leaves is most noticeable during early growth.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs during summer months with tiny clusters of inconspicuous flowers. This is the best time to see the plant at full size and identify the leaf shape clearly.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open, releasing smooth brown seeds. Foliage may take on more yellowish tones before dying back.
seasonality.winter: As a perennial, the above-ground portions die back, leaving only underground parts to survive New England's cold winters.

funFact: This plant is so rare in New England that there's only been ONE confirmed sighting in the entire region - making it rarer here than finding a four-leaf clover, which occurs about once in every 5,000 plants!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other spurges, but the combination of oval, toothed leaves and hairy texture helps distinguish it. Remember: 'Eggleaf = oval leaves with tiny teeth' - most other spurges have either smooth-edged leaves or completely different leaf shapes like the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'spurge,' these plants are unrelated to the similar-sounding 'scourge.' The spurge family includes the familiar Christmas poinsettia, and all family members share that distinctive milky sap that can cause skin irritation - always handle spurges with care.
compareHints: Unlike cypress spurge with its needle-like leaves or spotted spurge that grows as a low mat, eggleaf spurge stands upright with distinctly oval, toothed leaves. While petty spurge also has oval leaves, they lack the fine teeth along the edges that make eggleaf spurge distinctive. The hairy texture also sets it apart from most other New England spurges, which tend to be smooth.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike other spurges in New England that typically have broader, more conventional leaves, cypress spurge is instantly recognizable by its needle-like foliage.
Among New England's spurges, spotted spurge is unique for its ground-hugging mat formation and distinctly spotted leaves.
Among New England's spurges, seaside sandmat is unique in its completely prostrate, mat-forming habit and coastal habitat.
Among New England spurges, slender leafy spurge is distinguished by its tall, narrow growth form and lance-shaped leaves.
Among New England's spurges, nodding spurge is distinguished by its prostrate, mat-forming growth and drooping flower clusters.
Unlike other New England spurges which are mostly weedy annuals with thin leaves, Donkey Tail is a perennial succulent with thick, fleshy foliage.
Among New England's sandmat spurges, Wormseed Sandmat is distinguished by its perfectly circular growth pattern and distinctively ridged seeds.
Among New England spurges, caper spurge is unique for its large size and architectural growth habit - most other spurges are low-growing weeds or small garden plants.
Unlike the tall, weedy leafy spurge or the ground-hugging spotted spurge, cushion spurge maintains a perfectly rounded, compact form.
Among New England spurges, petty spurge is one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
Flowering spurge towers over most of its spurge relatives in New England, which tend to be low, mat-forming plants like spotted spurge or cypress spurge.
Snow-on-the-mountain is easily distinguished from other New England spurges by its distinctive white-margined leaves - most other spurges in our region have plain green foliage.

Leafy spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its tall, upright growth and dense leafy appearance - most of its relatives like spotted spurge and prostrate sandmat are low, sprawling plants.
Among New England spurges, graceful spurge stands out for its relatively tall, upright growth compared to the ground-hugging spotted spurge or prostrate sandmat.
Among New England's spurges, thymeleaf sandmat is distinguished by its ground-hugging mat formation and tiny thyme-like leaves.
Sweet spurge stands out from other New England spurges by its clumping perennial growth habit and relatively large, oval leaves.
Among New England spurges, green poinsettia stands out for its distinctly hairy, toothed leaves - most other spurges have smooth or nearly smooth leaves.
Unlike the needle-like leaves of cypress spurge or the spotted stems of spotted spurge, David's spurge has broader, toothed leaves arranged in opposite pairs.
Unlike other New England spurges that have broader, more typical-looking leaves, grassleaf spurge's ultra-narrow foliage makes it unique in the region.
Among New England's spurges, prostrate sandmat is uniquely flat-growing - most other spurges like cypress spurge or flowering spurge grow upright.
Compared to other New England spurges, Florida hammock sandmat is distinguished by its exceptionally small size and extremely low, tight mat-forming habit.
Matted sandmat is flatter and more perfectly mat-forming than most other spurges in our region.
Among New England's spurges, ribseed sandmat is distinguished by its extremely rare occurrence and the ribbed seeds that give it its name.
